corrected_value.title: Individual differences in simultaneous perceptual compensation for coarticulatory and lexical cues
corrected_value.title_o: Individual differences in simultaneous perceptual compensation for coarticulatory and lexical cues

decisions.quote:
This
study explores the nature of this individual variation through three speech sound categorization
tasks: one where both lexical and coarticulatory biases are present simultaneously for the /s-ʃ/
sibilants, a replication of Lai et al. (2022), the second where only lexical bias is present for /ɛ/-/ɪ/
vowels, and finally /d/-/g/ stops following /r/ or /l/ coarticulatory biasing contexts.
Across 89 native Canadian English listeners, we replicated the within-task trade-off between lexical
and coarticulatory effects (r= -0.19), weaker but consistent with Lai et al. (2022).

Vanguard, 8, 29-39, doi:10.1515/lingvan-2020-0040) as the original study replicated in Task 1 and tested for cross-task generalizability.

decisions.reason: The primary source (Zhai, Clayards, & Sonderegger, 10.1121/10.0042222) explicitly formulates Research Question 2 (Section II, lines 1074-1078) to empirically re-test the negative individual-level trade-off between lexical reliance and acoustic continuum use reported by Giovannone & Theodore (2023), and tests this specific published finding with new participant data (N = 89) in Task 1 and Task 2 (Section V.B, lines 2436-2450; Section V.B.2, lines 2879-2915; Section VI, lines 3143-3163). The reference list (lines 4105-4106) establishes the exact bibliographic identity: Giovannone, N., and Theodore, R. M. (2023), 'Do individual differences in lexical reliance reflect states or traits?,' Cognition, 232, 105320 (doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105320). The only shipped row for this work is input_row_index 993 (Lai, Wade, & Tamminga, 2022, Linguistics Vanguard, 10.1515/lingvan-2020-0040, which corresponds to target_index 0 and was confirmed in the prior adjudication file 7e51318dbb3bf89a9a482b8875991f4bb42320518fb2d8f6199855688fa555c1.json; no prior state file exists). Giovannone & Theodore (2023) is a completely independent original work by different authors in a different journal and is genuinely omitted from the shipped dataset.

decisions.location: Abstract, p. 1, lines 17-29 (and Section V.A, p. 13, lines 2124-2126; Section VI, p. 19, lines 3052-3068)
decisions.quote:
This
study explores the nature of this individual variation through three speech sound categorization
tasks: one where both lexical and coarticulatory biases are present simultaneously for the /s-ʃ/
sibilants, a replication of Lai et al. (2022), the second where only lexical bias is present for /ɛ/-/ɪ/
vowels, and finally /d/-/g/ stops following /r/ or /l/ coarticulatory biasing contexts.
Across 89 native Canadian English listeners, we replicated the within-task trade-off between lexical
and coarticulatory effects (r= -0.19), weaker but consistent with Lai et al. (2022). There was no
evidence for a trade-off across tasks; a joint Bayesian model that estimated individual-level
correlations across tasks showed that lexical and coarticulatory effects were not credibly related.
Participants’ consistency in categorizing the acoustic continuum (effect of continuum step) was
consistent across tasks. Overall, the findings suggest that while trade-off patterns can be replicated
within specific tasks, they are not robust across tasks, indicating possible task-specific effects or
contrast-specific perceptual strategies.
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 993 and blind target 0 coded 'mixed', but every published empirical finding of Lai, Wade, & Tamminga (2022, DOI: 10.1515/lingvan-2020-0040) was replicated in Task 1 (the sole task replicating Lai et al., 2022): (1) the group-level lexical and coarticulatory biasing effects and stronger lexical bias ('These results replicate the original results in Lai et al. showing both biasing effects and a stronger effect for lexical bias', Section V.A, lines 2124-2126), and (2) the focal within-task negative trade-off between lexical reliance and coarticulatory compensation (r = -0.19, PD = 0.95, 'weaker but consistent with Lai et al. (2022)', Abstract lines 22-23; Section VI lines 3055-3068; Section VII lines 3618-3625). Per the codebook, a weaker effect size that the authors treat as replicating/consistent is coded 'successful', not 'mixed'. None of the three putative grounds for 'mixed' is a failed comparison against a published finding of Lai et al. (2022): (a) Tasks 2 (Colby et al., 2018 vowel Ganong task) and 3 (Mann, 1980 liquid-stop coarticulation task) are explicitly introduced as a novel multi-task extension testing whether the single-task trade-off generalizes across separate tasks and phonetic contrasts as predicted by the broader processing-style theoretical account (RQ1b, Section III lines 815-871, 922-925; Section VI lines 3069-3089), and under the codebook and review instructions, extension tests and qualifications of general theory do not alter the replication outcome of the original study; (b) the correlation between continuum-step sensitivity and coarticulatory bias in Task 1 was explicitly not investigated in the published Lai et al. (2022) paper ('Although correlations involving continuum step effect was not investigated in Lai et al. (2022), our own reanalysis of their data (available at https://osf.io/kefn4/) found a moderate positive correlation between the use of continuum and coarticulatory bias in perception (r = 0.32, p = 0.04)', Section II.D, lines 787-805), so the absence of that correlation in Task 1 (Section VI, line 3194) is a contrast against the present authors' own newly conducted reanalysis within this paper rather than a published finding of Lai et al. (2022); and (c) Endnote 2 (lines 3779-3788, with its displaced opening fragment at lines 3816-3817) describes a discarded N=10 preliminary stimulus-development pilot on a /da/-/ga/ continuum rather than a replication test of Lai et al. (2022).
